clue.text: Change needed to make this army unit work!

definitions.text: Change needed to make this army unit work!

parts.words: Change needed to make this army unit work!
parts.note: the gambling device swallows coins (change) before it will play, and its nickname is a one-armed bandit, so 'army unit' is a pun on a single arm

explanation.surface: A sergeant complains that a regiment needs reform before it can function.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Army unit' looks military but means something with one arm: the one-armed bandit of a pub or arcade, which needs loose change put in to work.
explanation.definitionFit: A coin-operated gambling machine is nicknamed a one-armed bandit and only runs when fed with loose coins.

clue.text: Knocked down in imperfect sounding way

indicators.note: the clue asks for a word that sounds like the word for imperfect, so what is said aloud matters

parts.note: something imperfect is flawed

explanation.surface: A boxer was knocked down because of a technical failing in his style.
explanation.walkthrough: In a non-rhotic British accent FLAWED and FLOORED are said the same way.
explanation.definitionFit: A boxer knocked down is put on the canvas, sent to the ground.

clue.text: Rugby Union paint splashed all over these coaches

indicators.note: paint splashed all over is scattered, so these letters are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone daubs rugby team coaches with paint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coaches' suggests sports trainers, but these are railway carriages. An up train runs towards London or the main terminus.
explanation.definitionFit: A train heading towards the capital is a set of railway carriages, which are called coaches.

clue.text: Fastest gun of highest social position

definitions.meaning: a gunslinger who pulls his pistol from the holster quickest is the best at drawing
an idiom for the upper class, the best people

explanation.definitionFit: The quickest gunfighter is the best at drawing his weapon, and the phrase also means belonging to the top of society.

clue.text: Lofty sort of wit?

definitions.meaning: lofty here means up in the loft, a room under the roof
the refined wit associated with ancient Athens is called by this adjective

explanation.definitionFit: The room in the roof space is a loft, and the adjective for Athens names a refined, elegant style of humour.

clue.text: Concealed gaol crazy nobleman in Spain

parts.note: concealed means hid

indicators.note: crazy suggests the letters of the word gaol are scrambled out of order

explanation.surface: A Spanish aristocrat is hidden away in a madhouse of a prison.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gaol' is the British spelling of jail; 'crazy' is the anagram signal. A hidalgo is a minor Spanish noble.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the lower Spanish nobility holds this title.

clue.text: Tell of Scottish isle rising against the heartless

indicators.note: in a down clue rising means the island name is read from bottom to top

parts.note: Arran is an island in the Firth of Clyde, Scotland

indicators.note: a heartless word loses its middle letter, so the centre of the word the goes

explanation.surface: Someone recounts a story about a Scottish island rebelling against cruelty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rising' turns ARRAN into NARRA; 'heartless' takes the middle H out of THE, leaving TE.
explanation.definitionFit: To recount a story is to relate it, giving an account.

clue.text: Belted wealthy commuters?

parts.note: the prosperous Surrey suburbs where City financiers live are called the 'belt' of their trade, so 'belted' means living in that belt rather than hit

explanation.surface: Rich commuters get thumped on the train.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Belted' suggests a beating; the stockbroker belt is the affluent commuter area outside London, chiefly Surrey.
explanation.definitionFit: City share dealers famously commute from the leafy Surrey suburbs named after their profession.

clue.text: Dance that has the deuce of a small pace

parts.note: a deuce is a two in cards or dice
a step is a small pace

explanation.surface: A dance whose footwork is the very devil of a short stride.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the deuce' reads as a mild oath, the devil, but here it is the two of cards.
explanation.definitionFit: A ballroom dance in duple time with sliding steps.

clue.text: Turbulent current — it returns by day, demolishing pier

indicators.note: the word it returns, so it is read backwards
demolishing the pier breaks it up, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A violent current comes back each day and wrecks the seaside pier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returns' turns IT into TI; 'demolishing' rearranges PIER into ERIP; 'by' joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A rip is a stretch of rough water caused by opposing tidal flows.

clue.text: Crowd largely affected where reporters sit

parts.note: to crowd is to press, to push together

indicators.note: affected means altered, so the letters of the word largely are rearranged

explanation.surface: A big crowd is moved by events in the place reserved for journalists.
explanation.walkthrough: 'affected' rearranges LARGELY into GALLERY.
explanation.definitionFit: The seats in a parliament or court reserved for journalists.

clue.text: Pirates unfinished tune we hear

definitions.note: read as 'Pirate's', pirate is, a single sea robber

indicators.note: we hear points to a word that sounds like the phrase, rather than spells it

parts.note: coarse means unrefined or unfinished, and an air is a tune

explanation.surface: A pirate crew leaves a song half sung.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfinished' sounds like a tune cut short, but it gives COARSE (rough, unpolished); COARSE AIR said aloud matches the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A Barbary privateer or sea raider, so a robber on the high seas.

clue.text: Studio-pieces in one?

parts.note: an artwork made in a studio from many scraps of paper or cloth stuck down together on one surface

explanation.surface: A question about several works produced in a single studio.
explanation.definitionFit: A picture made by gluing assorted fragments onto a backing, many bits in a single work.

clue.text: Unhealthy quarters in former state of West Germany

parts.note: unhealthy means bad, as in bad for you
E and N are two compass points, quarters of the compass

explanation.surface: Unwholesome living quarters in an old West German state.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quarters' sounds like lodgings, but compass points (here east and north) are quarters in crosswords.
explanation.definitionFit: A south-western region, merged in 1952 into Baden-Württemberg.

clue.text: Farm-workers who walked on air?

parts.note: farm hands who drove carts rode instead of walking, so they went on air in the sense of moving above the ground

explanation.surface: Farm hands were so happy they seemed to float along.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Walked on air' means felt elated; the cart drivers sat high up on their vehicles instead of going on foot.
explanation.definitionFit: Farm labourers in charge of horse-drawn carts were named after the vehicles they drove.

clue.text: Top gear for army drivers?

parts.note: top gear means clothing worn on top, a heavy military overcoat, not the highest setting of a gearbox

explanation.surface: A question about which gear military drivers use at speed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top gear' suggests the fastest gear of a vehicle; it is outer clothing, the heavy coat of a soldier.
explanation.definitionFit: A heavy long overcoat, standard military outerwear worn over the uniform.

clue.text: Stuff that is left to defile

parts.note: what is left is left over
a defile is a narrow pass, a gorge

explanation.surface: Material left behind is used to pollute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'defile' reads as a verb, to spoil, but it is the noun, a narrow valley.
explanation.definitionFit: To stuff oneself is to eat to excess, gorging too much.

clue.text: It grows tough around seaport

indicators.note: around means the letters of the word seaport are moved round into a new order

explanation.surface: A hardy plant grows near a harbour town.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' rearranges SEAPORT.
explanation.definitionFit: A tough wiry grass of Spain and North Africa, used for paper and rope.

clue.text: Possibly caring about English nose that is straight

definitions.note: the answer is an adjective describing a nose of that kind

indicators.note: about places one piece around another
possibly suggests the letters of the word caring could be arranged another way

explanation.surface: Perhaps kind-hearted, an English person has a classic straight nose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Possibly' rearranges CARING into GRCIAN, and 'about' puts it around E.
explanation.definitionFit: Classical Greek statues show a profile with a straight bridge running from the forehead.

clue.text: A"'is so transposed as a musical alternative

indicators.note: transposed means the letters of the phrase are put in reverse order

explanation.surface: A musician reads a phrase written backwards as an optional passage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'transposed' reverses A IS SO; the musical sense of transposing misleads.
explanation.definitionFit: An Italian term printed in scores marking an alternative, often easier, passage the player may use instead.

clue.text: Urban work-paid out by noon

parts.note: op, short for opus, is a musical work

indicators.note: out means the letters of the word paid are put out of order

explanation.surface: City labour gets paid off by midday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' rearranges PAID into PIDA; 'by' joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A Latin-derived word for a town-dweller or of a town, used at Eton for a boy boarding in the town.

clue.text: Observer of Lifemanship originally?

parts.note: Lifemanship was written by Stephen Potter: take his first initial with his surname

explanation.surface: A reviewer of a well-known humorous book.
explanation.walkthrough: Stephen Potter wrote the 1950 humour book Lifemanship; 'originally' takes the initial of his first name, put before his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who looks out for and notices things, like a lookout or birdwatcher.

clue.text: Intimate 2,perhaps

definitions.meaning: to intimate is to state or put into words
the answer to 2 down is a train, and a fast one is an example of this

explanation.definitionFit: To intimate is to make known, put into words, and a fast non-stopping train is an example of a railway service.

clue.text: Turnip we'd plant in home counties

indicators.note: plant in means set one piece inside another

parts.note: the Home Counties around London lie in the south-east, SE
we'd taken as written without its apostrophe

explanation.surface: A gardener says we would set a turnip in the counties near London.
explanation.walkthrough: The Home Counties are the counties surrounding London, in the south-east of England.
explanation.definitionFit: The yellow root vegetable called rutabaga in America is a kind of turnip.

clue.text: Beds highest ground

parts.note: the uppermost layer of earth in garden beds

explanation.surface: Bedfordshire's highest point.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beds' looks like the abbreviation for Bedfordshire, an English county, but means flower beds.
explanation.definitionFit: The upper layer of earth, the part dug and planted in a garden.

clue.text: Packers' subject — hard-pressed tail-ender?

parts.note: a small fish that canning factories squash tight into tins, tail to head

explanation.surface: A cricketer batting last is under pressure from a team called the Packers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tail-ender' suggests a last-batting cricketer; the little fish is packed hard into a tin with tails alternating.
explanation.definitionFit: A small oily fish famously packed tight in tins.

clue.text: Les trod carefully-he's getting on a bit!

indicators.note: carefully suggests the letters of Les trod are treated with care and arranged anew

explanation.surface: Les walked cautiously because he is ageing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'carefully' rearranges LES TROD.
explanation.definitionFit: An elderly person, someone getting on in years.

clue.text: Does he produce the top range in the shop!

definitions.text: Does he produce the top range in the shop!

parts.words: Does he produce the top range in the shop!
parts.note: a male alto sings the highest range, and the shop surface where goods are served suggests the first part

explanation.surface: A shopkeeper asks whether a salesman offers the best goods.
explanation.walkthrough: 'top range' looks like premium stock in a shop; it is the highest male voice, a shop counter plus a singing voice.
explanation.definitionFit: A male singer whose voice reaches the alto range, above a tenor.
